title.en: Say where the anatomy geometry came from

summary: Distinguish artist-sculpted anatomy from imaging-derived geometry, and never let stylised meshes carry clinical claims.
objective: Match the strength of an anatomical claim to the provenance of the geometry that carries it.
applies_when: An anatomical model is presented for teaching, patient communication or reference.
Geometry is imported from an asset library or generated by sculpting.
Measurements, sizes or spatial relationships might be read as clinically meaningful.
intent_signals: use it for a patient explainer
example_prompts: Build an anatomy explainer and be clear about what it can and cannot show.
Use this asset for teaching and state its limitations.
negative_signals: Fictional creatures and stylised characters, where no anatomical claim exists.
Data-derived scientific visualisation with documented acquisition, which has its own stronger provenance.
not_for: Fictional creatures and stylised characters, where no anatomical claim exists.
Data-derived scientific visualisation with documented acquisition, which has its own stronger provenance.

principles: Rendering quality is independent of anatomical fidelity. A beautifully shaded sculpt and a segmented scan look equally authoritative and are not equally trustworthy.
Provenance determines what can be claimed: a sculpt supports naming and relations, imaging-derived geometry can support shape and size within its acquisition limits, and neither supports diagnosis.
Measurement is the boundary that matters most. Adding a ruler to a stylised mesh converts an illustration into a false measurement instrument.
Individual variation means even accurate geometry represents one subject or one atlas, not every body.
implementation: Record the origin of each anatomical asset with the artifact: sculpted, atlas-derived, imaging-derived, or generated, along with licence and any modification.
Match the offered interactions to the provenance: naming, relations and layer reveal for sculpts; measurement only where the geometry supports it.
State the intended audience and use, and state plainly that a teaching model is not a diagnostic or planning tool.
Where scale is illustrative, label it, and avoid a units readout that implies measurement.
Keep the sourced claim list and the geometry provenance next to each other so a later edit can be re-checked.
observable_checks: Ask what would change if this model were used for a real decision; if the answer is nothing, the disclosure is missing.
Look for measurement affordances such as rulers, coordinates or volumes on geometry that cannot support them.
Confirm the asset provenance is recorded rather than remembered.
Check that stylised proportions are disclosed where a viewer might read them as typical.

creative_affordances: Stylised, illustrative anatomy is often the better teaching choice; the rule asks for disclosure, not photorealism.
Combining an accurate skeleton with schematic soft tissue is legitimate when the mixture is described.
known_limits: Authored disclosure guidance; it certifies no asset and evaluates no imaging pipeline.
It provides no medical, diagnostic or regulatory advice.
